passage: "It's all in your head, Bhavna. Just be strong," her father said, not looking up from the fertiliser receipts. Her mother nodded and passed her a plate. Bhavna carried it to the courtyard and did not eat. Home from college for the break, she had barely slept in weeks and cried in the bathroom with the tap running, and the one sentence she had finally managed had been waved away like smoke. She felt small and foolish. For two days she said nothing. Then she walked to the school and found Kunal Sir, who had taught her in Class Ten. She told him exactly what was happening: no sleep, no appetite, no interest in anything. "What you feel is real," he said. "Let me come and speak to your parents, and we can go to the health centre together."

qa.q: Who had taught Bhavna in Class Ten?
How did Bhavna feel after her father's reply?
qa.a: Dismissed, small and foolish, as if the sentence she had managed was waved away like smoke.

qa.q: Why did going to Kunal Sir with specifics help?
qa.a: It gave her concrete things to describe and brought a respected adult ally who could speak to her parents and go to the health centre with her.

qa.q: How might Bhavna's father have seen his own words?
qa.a: He may have thought he was encouraging her to be strong, without realising they made her feel dismissed.

grounding: Family dismisses her pain as 'all in your head'; she feels dismissed, then returns with specifics and an ally.

passage:
The joint family in Nashik had one landline, one TV and no privacy. Jeevan waited until the house was asleep, then told his father on the terrace that he hadn't slept properly in two months and couldn't concentrate at all.

"It's all in your mind," his father said. "Be strong. In my time nobody had these problems." He went back downstairs.

Jeevan sat on the cold tiles, feeling invisible. Part of him wanted to stop asking.

Instead, on Monday, he went to the college counsellor and asked for help explaining it. The counsellor wrote a short note in plain words: what Jeevan had been going through, and that it was real and treatable.

On Sunday Jeevan's uncle Hemant, a teacher whom his father respected, sat with them both. Hemant read the note aloud. His father listened, frowning. Then he said, "What do you need from us?"

qa.q: Where did Jeevan tell his father about his problems?
qa.a: Jeevan told his father on the terrace, after the house was asleep.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when his father went back downstairs?
qa.a: Jeevan felt dismissed and invisible, and was tempted to stop asking for help.

qa.q: How did Jeevan try again, and why did it work better?
qa.a: Jeevan got a note with specifics from the counsellor and brought in uncle Hemant, an ally his father respected, so his father actually listened.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's father have seen the problem at first?
qa.a: Jeevan's father seemed to see it as weakness, because in his time such problems were not talked about.

grounding: The story shows a young man whose family dismisses his distress, trying again with specifics and a respected ally instead of giving up.

passage:
"Arre, Ganga, it's all in your head. Just be strong, eat properly," her mother said, stirring the dal in their Kolkata flat. "Your cousin cleared her exams without all this drama."

Ganga went to her room and sat on the bed, shaking. She had spent a week working up the courage to say she was crying every day and couldn't get out of bed some mornings.

She messaged Keerthana: "Told Ma. She said it's in my head." Keerthana replied, "It's real whether she gets it or not. Want me to come with you to Dr Bose?"

On Saturday they went to the family doctor. Ganga described exactly what was happening: the crying, the mornings, the not eating. Dr Bose listened, then said, "Bring your mother next time. I'll explain it to her."

The following week her mother came, and asked quietly, "How long has it been like this?"

qa.q: What was Ganga's mother stirring when she spoke?
What was Ganga feeling after her mother's reply, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Ganga felt dismissed and hurt; she sat on her bed shaking after a week of building courage.

qa.q: What would you advise someone whose family says "it's all in your head"?
qa.a: Keep asking, describe exactly what is happening, and bring an ally such as a doctor who can explain it, as Ganga did.

qa.q: How might Ganga's mother see things differently by the end?
qa.a: After the doctor explained, her mother seems concerned rather than dismissive, asking quietly how long it had been going on.

grounding: The story shows a young woman whose family dismisses her pain, trying again with specifics and a doctor as an ally.
